You don't need to pay for AI API keys anymore.

Instead, use this free GitHub repo called free-llm-api-resources, and it lists down every free API provider out there.

It gives you free access to top models like Kimi, DeepSeek, Gemini, and more, all for completely free.

You just pick a provider like OpenRouter, NVIDIA NIM, or Google AI Studio, generate your API key.

Some providers give you more room than others though.

OpenRouter gives you up to 1,000 requests a day once you add a small lifetime top-up.

NVIDIA NIM gives you 40 requests a minute with just phone verification.

Google AI Studio is another solid one, since it gives you access to Gemini models with generous daily limits, and it doesn't require any payment info at all to get started.

There's also a second list in the repo for providers that hand out trial credits instead of fully free access.

Fireworks, Nebius, and Hyperbolic all give you a small credit balance to test bigger models before committing to anything.

So if you're building an agent that calls a model constantly, or you just want to try five different providers before picking a favorite, this repo saves you the trouble of hunting each one down individually.

Perfect for AI agents, side projects, or just testing things out without spending a dollar.

Your agent ran all night and wrote 30,000 lines of code. Every check passed. The app was broken. The loop didn't fail — your system did, because nothing in it could stop and ask if you were still solving the right problem. You already did the smart thing and split one agent into a team: a planner, a builder, a reviewer. That's the graph. But connecting agents isn't the same as putting someone in charge. The fix isn't a smarter model — it's a governance layer, an operating system for your agents. And the part you can build today is simple: every decision in your system has exactly one owner.

→ Countable things belong to CODE — budget limits, retry counts, valid JSON, tests passing; never ask a model to check what an IF statement can
→ Ambiguous things belong to the MODEL — why did this fail, the plan or the reviewer; let it diagnose, never let it decide alone
→ The mission belongs to YOU — not an approve button, the one person who owns what "done" actually means
→ That overnight disaster didn't need more intelligence; it needed code to stop the bleeding, a model to say why, and a human holding the goal
→ You already built half an operating system by accident — checkpoints, retries, permissions; the other half you build on purpose
→ A graph connects your agents. An operating system runs them.

fagSVgEtU2E.description:
The Demon Core was a 6.2 kilogram sphere of plutonium-gallium alloy, manufactured by the Manhattan Project in 1945 and originally intended for the third atomic bomb to be used against Japan. Japan surrendered before it was shipped, and the core remained at Los Alamos for testing.
On August 21, 1945, physicist Harry Daghlian was alone at the Omega Site, stacking tungsten carbide bricks around the core to study how close it could get to criticality. As he placed the final brick, neutron detectors indicated the assembly was going supercritical. He pulled his hand back, the brick slipped from his grip, and fell directly into the assembly. A flash of blue light filled the room. Daghlian dismantled the assembly by hand to stop the reaction, receiving an estimated whole-body dose of 290 to 310 rem, roughly 3 sieverts. He died 25 days later from acute radiation syndrome, the first person in history killed by a criticality accident.
Experiments with the core continued. On May 21, 1946, exactly nine months later, physicist Louis Slotin was performing a similar demonstration, holding a beryllium reflector dome apart from the core using the blade of a screwdriver rather than the required safety shims, a practice Enrico Fermi had specifically warned him would get him killed within a year. The screwdriver slipped. The dome closed. The room lit up blue again. Slotin, standing closest to the assembly, received an estimated dose of around 880 rem, roughly 8.8 sieverts, one of the most severe acute radiation exposures ever recorded in a survivable timeframe. He died 9 days later.
Remarkably, both accidents occurred on a Tuesday, both on the 21st of the month, and both men died in the same hospital room at the Los Alamos base hospital.
After Slotin's death, the core was permanently retired. It was melted down in the summer of 1946 and its plutonium recycled into other weapon cores. It was never assembled again.
Source: Atomic Heritage Foundation, Nuclear Museum. American Physical Society, This Month in Physics History (2014). Wikipedia, Harry Daghlian. Nevada Technical Associates, The Demon Core.
#DemonCore #ManhattanProject #LouisSlotin #RadiationSickness #CriticalityAccident

Hey everyone, In this video, we are going to talk about Transactional Outbox Pattern and how it works. The transactional outbox pattern guarantees that a local database update and the publishing of a message to an event broker (like Kafka) occur together atomically. It avoids the "dual-write" problem by storing outgoing messages in an "outbox" table in the same database, allowing a separate relay to publish them asynchronously.

p1aJ-xLkfVI.description:
The black-footed cat is the smallest wild cat in Africa, weighing barely 1 to 3 kilograms, small enough to hold in one hand. It is also, by hunting success rate, the deadliest cat on the planet.
According to research by Panthera's Luke Hunter and field studies using radio collars, the black-footed cat has a predation success rate of around 60 percent, roughly three times higher than a lion's, which succeeds in only 20 to 25 percent of its hunting attempts. In a single night, it kills between 10 and 14 rodents, birds, or small reptiles, averaging a successful kill about every 50 minutes. Smithsonian Magazine reported that in one night, this cat kills more prey than a leopard does in six months.
This is not a demonstration of skill for its own sake. The black-footed cat has an extremely fast metabolism, forcing it to hunt almost continuously through the night just to sustain itself. It consumes close to one-fifth of its own body weight in a single night. Scaled to human terms, a 70 kilogram person would need to eat roughly 14 kilograms of food in one sitting to match that.
The cat hunts using three distinct techniques: fast pursuit through grass, slow stalking, and motionless sit-and-wait ambush near burrow entrances, sometimes holding still for up to two hours before striking. Despite its size, it can leap up to 1.4 metres to catch birds mid-flight and travel between 5 and 16 kilometres a night in search of prey.
Its appearance has nothing to do with its behaviour. Evolution built a compact, efficient predator, and camouflaged it as something harmless.
Source: Guinness World Records, Most Successful Feline Predator. LiveScience, Adorable Remorseless Killing Machine Is World's Deadliest Cat (2018). Smithsonian Magazine, This Petite Cat Is the World's Deadliest (2018).

If you’re not, you’re already falling behind.

Attention Is All You Need.
Chain of Thought.
RAG.
ReAct.
Every major breakthrough in AI was a research paper before it became a product.
But I don’t start with the paper.
I start with a question.
Something like, “How do reasoning models actually work?”
Then I use Firecrawl’s Research Index to find the five best papers on that topic.
I paste them into Claude or ChatGPT and ask, “Where do these papers agree? Where do they disagree? And what’s genuinely new?”
Then I check GitHub.
If there’s a paper but no implementation, I’m skeptical.
Only then do I read the original paper, and I follow these two guides from Harvard and Stanford on how to read research papers.
That’s the entire process I follow.
The paper becomes the last step, not the first.

pKMFvQNvwps.description:
What if you could look at any firework and identify exactly which metal is burning inside it? Every color you see comes from a different chemical element, and the mechanism behind it is pure chemistry, not magic.
A firework shell is launched by a lifting charge of gunpowder. A timed fuse then ignites a second stage, bursting the shell open at altitude. Packed inside are small pellets called stars, each loaded with a specific metal compound. That metal is the entire secret behind the color.
When intense heat reaches the metal, its electrons absorb energy and jump to a higher energy level. The instant they fall back to their original state, they release a photon of light at one exact wavelength, a specific color. Because every element has a different energy gap between levels, every metal produces a distinct, characteristic color.
Strontium salts produce red. Sodium produces yellow. Barium produces green. Copper produces blue. Combining copper and strontium compounds produces purple. The bright white sparks come from metals like magnesium and titanium, which burn at such high temperatures that they glow white rather than any specific color.
Blue is considered the most difficult color to produce reliably. Copper compounds break down and lose their color-producing ability if the flame temperature rises too high, so achieving a clean, deep blue firework is regarded as a genuine mark of pyrotechnic skill.
Every firework display is, quite literally, a section of the periodic table burning in the sky.
Source: American Chemical Society, Chemistry of Fireworks. Compound Interest, The Chemistry of Firework Colours. Royal Society of Chemistry, Fireworks.

py_--ZJqxMM.description:
An object roughly the size of a four-story building is on a collision course with the Moon, and astronomers around the world are preparing to watch.

The object is the upper stage of a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket, catalogued as 2025-010D, launched on January 15, 2025 to carry two private lunar landers toward the Moon, Firefly Aerospace's Blue Ghost and ispace's Hakuto-R Mission 2. Once its job was done, the spent stage was left drifting through the Earth-Moon system rather than being deliberately disposed of. For over a year, the combined gravitational pull of Earth, the Moon, and the Sun, along with solar radiation pressure, continuously reshaped its orbit, until astronomer Bill Gray of Project Pluto calculated in September 2025 that impact with the Moon had become inevitable.

The upper stage, about 13.8 metres tall and weighing roughly 4 metric tons, will strike the lunar surface at approximately 8,700 kilometres per hour, more than seven times the speed of sound. Because the Moon has no atmosphere, there is nothing to burn the object up before impact. It will hit near Einstein Crater on the Moon's western limb, carving out a new crater estimated at 20 to 30 metres wide and throwing up a multi-kilometre plume of ejected dust.

Whether this will be visible from Earth is still uncertain among scientists. If the dust cloud is bright enough, ground and space-based telescopes could capture the impact in real time. The predicted window is 06:35 to 06:44 UTC on August 5, 2026, which is 12:05 to 12:14 PM IST.

This is a rare opportunity. No artificial object has ever been directly observed striking the Moon's sunlit side before, and scientists hope the event will provide real data on lunar subsurface structure and crater formation.

Source: Fernando, B. et al. (2026). Observational Planning for the 2026 August 5 Falcon 9 Upper Stage Lunar Impact. arXiv. Scientific American, A SpaceX Rocket Is About to Crash Into the Moon (2026). BBC Sky at Night Magazine (2026). EarthSky (2026).

You set up a local proxy on your Mac, connect it to your Codex login, and create an alias called claudex.
Now when you type claudex in your terminal, you get Claude Code’s entire interface, but with GPT-5.6 generating the responses.
Claude Code still handles the tools, file edits, subagents, and progress tracking.
GPT-5.6 just does the thinking.
And this experiment taught me something I wasn’t expecting.
The harness matters way more than the model.
Claude Code isn’t just a wrapper.
It decides how context flows, how tools get called, and how long-running threads stay alive.
Swap the model underneath, and the experience barely changes.
That’s how much the harness is doing.
But using Codex behind Claude Code is also like buying a great camera and only using it as a webcam.
You lose everything Codex does natively.
So I use both.
Claude Code when I want Claude Code.
Codex when I want Codex.

What happens when an AI model becomes so capable that other AI systems refuse to analyze its behavior?

In a recent AI cybersecurity benchmark, a pre-release version of OpenAI's GPT-5.6 reportedly identified a zero-day vulnerability, gained internet access within the test environment, and autonomously executed a 17,000-step attack chain during the evaluation.

But the most surprising part came afterward.

Researchers wanted to analyze the attack logs using commercial AI models. However, many models refused because the logs contained exploit payloads, and their safety systems couldn't reliably distinguish security analysis from generating offensive cyber content.

The team then turned to GLM 5.2, an open-weight AI model from Z.ai, running it locally. It was able to reconstruct and analyze the entire attack chain for forensic investigation.

The bigger takeaway isn't just about one model.

It's about a growing challenge in AI security:

Powerful AI systems are becoming more capable.
Safety filters can sometimes limit defensive analysis.
Open-weight models are increasingly important for cybersecurity research.

SLw2Ce950hs.description:
Most people assume the giant squid is the largest squid species in the ocean. It is not. That title belongs to the colossal squid, the heaviest invertebrate known to science, larger by mass than the giant squid despite being shorter in total length.
In March 2025, the Schmidt Ocean Institute's ROV SuBastian filmed a colossal squid alive in its natural habitat for the first time in history, near the South Sandwich Islands at a depth of 600 metres. But the individual captured on camera was only about 30 centimetres long, a juvenile. A fully grown adult can reach nearly 7 metres and weigh up to 500 kilograms, the scale of creature that once inspired sailors' stories of the Kraken. No adult has ever been filmed alive.
So how do scientists know adults exist at all? The evidence comes from sperm whales, the colossal squid's only known predator. Whales have been observed at the surface carrying scars from squid suckers, and in some cases, torn tentacle fragments still embedded in their skin. When sperm whale stomachs have been examined, they have contained squid beaks, the one part of the animal that cannot be digested, providing direct physical proof of predation on adult colossal squids.
Even locating the species would not answer every question. The colossal squid has the largest eyes of any known animal, roughly the size of a volleyball, believed to help it detect faint bioluminescence at a distance and spot an approaching sperm whale in complete darkness before being seen itself. Yet scientists still do not know whether it actively hunts or waits motionless as an ambush predator for prey to come within range.
By comparison, scientists consider the megalodon extinct largely because its distinctive bite marks have stopped appearing in the fossil and modern predation record. Colossal squid scars, by contrast, are still being found on sperm whales today. The species is alive, present, and largely unmapped.
Source: Schmidt Ocean Institute, First Live Sighting of a Colossal Squid (2025). Natural History Museum, Colossal Squid Facts. Te Papa Museum, Colossal Squid Research.

comments.author: @susmangugu
comments.text:
Here is a fact check of the claims made in the video "Here's How Much Water AI Consumes" by Varun Mayya (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uR2JDsLZS6I):
1. Water Footprint Comparisons (Burger, T-shirt, and AI Images)
Claim: Making one burger takes ~2,400 liters of water (equivalent to ~83,000 AI images), and a t-shirt takes ~2,700 liters (~94,000 AI images) [00:00].
Fact Check: Accurate in order of magnitude.
The Water Footprint Network estimates that an average 150g beef burger requires ~2,400 liters of water (accounting for feed, drinking water, and processing).
The UN Environment Programme (UNEP) estimates a cotton t-shirt requires approximately 2,700 liters of water across its lifecycle.
Based on per-prompt inference water consumption estimates (~0.026–0.03 liters per image generation/response), these comparative ratios align with published research estimates (such as those from UC Riverside and Washington University in St. Louis).
2. GPT-3 Training Water Consumption
Claim: In 2022, training a GPT-3 size model consumed roughly 700,000 liters of water [00:26].
Fact Check: Accurate.
This figure comes directly from a landmark 2023 study by researchers at UC Riverside and UT Arlington ("Making AI Less "Thirsty": Uncovering and Addressing the Secret Water Footprint of AI Models" by Shaolei Ren et al.). The study estimated that direct and indirect water consumption for training GPT-3 in Microsoft’s state-of-the-art US data centers was approximately 700,000 liters (around 185,000 gallons).
3. Inference Efficiency Improvement
Claim: Per-prompt inference has become significantly more efficient, dropping from ~10–50 ml in 2022 to ~0.26 ml (or fractions of a milliliter) per prompt [00:46].
Fact Check: Generally Accurate (Context-Dependent).
Early estimates for simple ChatGPT interactions (GPT-3) ranged between 20–50 ml of water per 20–50 questions. Optimizations in model architectures, quantization, specialized hardware (e.g., modern GPUs/TPUs), and software efficiency have drastically reduced the operational energy and cooling cost per prompt for smaller models. However, standard queries on massive, multimodal reasoning models can still consume higher amounts depending on sequence length and server load.
4. US Data Center Water Usage vs. Golf Courses and Crop Irrigation
Claim: All US data centers combined use roughly 65 billion liters of water per year, compared to far higher usage for crop irrigation, golf courses (~10–18x more), and paper mills [01:08].
Fact Check: Accurate Context / Valid Perspective.
Data Center Usage: US data center water consumption estimates generally fall between 50 billion to 100 billion liters annually for direct cooling and indirect electricity production water footprint.
Comparisons: Agricultural irrigation in the US accounts for over 100 trillion liters per year. Golf course irrigation in the US consumes an estimated 1.5 to 2.0 billion gallons per day (~2 trillion liters/year), which is roughly 15 to 20 times the total water consumed by data centers.
5. Water Recycling in Modern Data Centers
Claim: Recent AI data centers recycle the same water again and again with near-zero wastage [01:50].
Fact Check: Mostly True with Technical Nuance.
Modern data centers increasingly use closed-loop cooling systems (chilled water recirculated through evaporators/chillers) or advanced air cooling / direct-to-chip liquid cooling systems.
However, evaporative cooling towers (which dissipate heat into the atmosphere) still consume non-recycled water via evaporation. Major tech companies (Google, Microsoft, Meta) have committed to becoming "water positive" by 2030 by replenishing more water than they consume and transitioning toward zero-water cooling solutions.

Claude Code tips from the creator of Claude Code. Boris Cherny's own workflow as a Claude Code tutorial: how to use Claude Code on today's models, what to delete from your setup, and which Claude Code skills still earn their place. Claude Code for beginners and pros.

Try Buzzy Canvas at https://shr.pn/buzzy-now and bring your entire AI video workflow into one place.

Community with All Resources: http://ailabspro.io

The Roundup, our daily newsletter covering the AI stories that matter. Join now: https://www.theroundup.so/


Boris Cherny, the creator of Claude Code, said in an interview that even with models as capable as Fable 5, most people still use them the way they used Sonnet 3.5. So these aren't top Claude Code tips you apply once and forget. They're the pass you run every time a new model ships, from Anthropic Claude or anyone else, and this is how to use Claude in a real Claude Code workflow.

Delete your setup when a new model ships
- Anthropic cut about 80% of Claude Code's own system prompt when Opus 5 shipped. Your claude.md gets read on every single turn.
- The usage and context commands show what your setup costs you. Safe mode turns it all off so you can see how the model does without it.
- The rule: would Claude have worked this out on its own? If yes, delete it. The doctor command trims by exactly that rule.

Evals, the thing Boris says people get most wrong
- An eval is a fixed check that decides when work is done, and it has to be strict enough to fail.
- Boris had Claude rebuild the Claude desktop app in Swift and compare screenshots pixel by pixel. It's been running over two weeks. Without a check like that, an agent stalls out in an hour.

Prompting
- Say what you want, not how to do it. Boris says experienced engineers are the worst at this.
- Hand an agent an inspiration image and you get a near copy. Describe it instead and it works out the approach itself.

Where things go
- Prompt, then claude.md, then a skill, then MCP only when Claude genuinely can't reach the information.

Beyond one prompt
- We don't recommend dynamic workflows. The Bun rewrite cost roughly $165,000 at API pricing and still shipped nineteen breakages.
- Routines are what you'll actually use: recurring cloud jobs that keep running after you close the laptop. Anthropic runs twenty to thirty a day.

This is AI coding the way a software company runs it, so if you're into vibe coding but want coding with AI that holds up, these Claude Code beginner tips are where to start. Everything shown is Claude Code, not Claude Cowork, and the routines are where it turns into real AI automation. All our skills and setups live in AI Labs Pro.

ZE1KEgsm_80.description:
Uber just shipped an AI agent that builds your whole grocery cart from a photo of a handwritten list — and the interesting part for builders is how little the LLM actually does.

Their real architecture is a multi-prompt state graph, and most of the boxes are plain deterministic code. The LLM only handles the fuzzy stuff: reading what you meant, judging which product fits. Everything that has to be correct — prices, arithmetic, availability, the cart total — is code the model never touches.

→ The planner LLM doesn't "go shopping" — it emits a structured CartPlan (item, search_terms, item_context, price constraints), then hands it to code
→ "12 eggs" resolves to one carton of twelve via a deterministic quantity step, not free LLM arithmetic
→ A deterministic guardrail can veto a bad output and fall back before it ever reaches your cart
→ The lesson: when an agent is unreliable, the fix usually isn't a bigger model — it's taking responsibility away from the model and moving anything exact into code

The rule to steal: LLM handles meaning, code handles truth.

Comment "CART" and I'll send you the full breakdown.
What's the one thing you'd never let an AI decide?

I don't have a programming degree, and never took formal education for IT or workflows. I learned it all myself from YouTube videos like you're watching now.

Have you ever tried creating a video ad from scratch? First, you need product photos, then a script, then someone to present it, then editing, then revisions. And after all that, there is still no guarantee the ad will perform well.

In this video, I test Creatify AI, an AI advertising platform designed to help create complete marketing ads from a product URL, product images, or a text description. Instead of only generating random videos, Creatify helps with research, messaging, scripts, voiceovers, avatars, visual scenes, ad structure, and final production.

Creating ads normally requires a lot of moving parts. You need copywriting, product images, voiceovers, actors or presenters, editing, and multiple creative versions for testing.

Even with AI tools, many marketers still jump between separate platforms to create one ad. One tool writes the script, another generates visuals, another creates a voiceover, and another edits the final video.

Creatify AI tries to simplify that by bringing the ad creation workflow into one platform. According to the script, Creatify can turn a product URL, images, or text description into ready-to-use video ads.

In the first test, I paste a product page URL directly into Creatify. The platform analyzes the product page, gathers information, and starts building a full ad structure. It generates marketing angles, scripts, voiceovers, visual scenes, and a complete video ad from a single link.

The next feature I test is the Creatify AI Agent. Instead of clicking through multiple menus, I describe the ad I want, such as an ad targeting small business owners who want to save time creating marketing content. The agent then helps with research, messaging, script generation, avatar selection, and ad production.

I also test the asset generator by uploading a basic product image and turning it into cleaner promotional visuals. This can be useful for brands or small businesses that do not have access to expensive product photography.

Another interesting part of Creatify is the ability to create a custom AI presenter. You can start with a text prompt, generate a character, turn that character into an avatar, and use that avatar as the presenter inside the ad.

For marketers, variation matters. Creatify can help generate multiple ad styles using the same product, such as UGC style, interview style, podcast style, and cinematic style. The message stays consistent while the presentation changes, which makes it easier to test different creative angles.

Creatify also gives users two ways to work. Beginners can use the chat-based workflow and let the AI handle most of the decisions. More advanced users can use the visual workflow editor to manually adjust different parts of the ad creation process.

After testing Creatify AI, the biggest strength is not just video generation. It is the way the platform combines scripting, visuals, avatars, assets, and production into one connected workflow.

Creatify probably will not replace a professional creative team completely, but for entrepreneurs, marketers, creators, ecommerce brands, and small businesses, it can reduce the time and effort needed to create video ads.

According to the script, Creatify also offers a free plan with free monthly credits, so you can test the platform and see how it fits your workflow.
